Ok. Here I've got two takes on website design. Tell me what you think we do. 


NATHAN DIRECT:
First and foremost... if we can just make the backend totally editable from the backend by me or assistants, that would be ideal since I only get a small allotment of "work" (and Sites is automatically "work") per *week*. If we can have live flow from the backend, we should be able to do live editing; I can write HTML and copy-paste code *myself* if I have to... no need for the value-add "Sites" instance except where we actually *need* it, or as a startup or lookover / optimize kind of role. 

We don't need this: Current H(s)H visual register · supplied project artwork
The "public notebook"... it's wonky-ish... [THUMB] + Title on open space. If nothing else, the title should be topped. Better, it should be followed by explanation. My prefered format generally for most things... especially navigatey things is all caps or small caps THING or DO THIS (no more than two or three, ideally short, words) then description below if needed. But equally crisp/terse/short. Maybe kinda like...

LIBRARY - Scientists | Specialists | Everyone
NEWS - The Theory | Related Stories | Archive
DRAFTS - Papers | Theory Work | Press Releases 
SEE SAT - Basics | Full Overview | Topics | Data
SEE H(s)H - Basics | Full Overview | Topics | Data

And generally, everything is point-of-use: What do you need on the front page?/What does one want from the first page?/How can the first page serve as self-triage?/How can the front page shhow the bredth and depth and variety and explore options?  > Say, we click into the library. *There* we say simply and prominently: This is a collection of primary documents, formatted for browsing. This is fully transparent research library; Click "RAW" to see the original. ... or better, just the former; the latter can live right under the "RAW" button. Or perhaps... and I kind of like this... we make the "library" itself almost an embedded sub-entity with letterhead: 

GLASS SAUSAGE FACTORY RESEARCH LIBRARY
Documents are preserved as primary sources, warts and all. 

Or just an option branch: 
RESEARCH LIBRARY - Curated? | Warts and all?

Or all or some of the above/something else? 

...or even a motto or something. 

Overall, our goal is: 

Very condensed. Very clear. Very organized. And then things like Podcast: What Is Thought Made Of? [SAT's Public Debut] ...stands out. Wayfinding isn't prose, prose isn't news, news isn't science. Different lanes, visually apparent. Maybe even push each subsection to draw the eye of a different kind of reader: Ah, pdf thumbnail... scientist goes there... ah, pictures... regular person goes there. ah, headlines... follower goes there ah, press releases... ah, faq... etc ...then *there* the branching/nav is logical *for that reader* 

Podcasts should have a better topic sort (this is a *little* hard because the intro isn't always direcly related... but it is *usually* of the same era, so its ~more related) we should probably have a (maybe auto) wide/narrow option(s) or reflows. And the "large text" should itself be LARGE, and the text should be GRANDMA if you click it. Otherwise, most of the text is just about right at this point.

We don't really need labels like "Paper A" and "Paper B". Too internal. Same with "Standing Return Cursor" ...makes no sense to an outsider. We're aiming for human readers... I think? ...mostly? And on that note... part of transparency is not using 'FIE' or *too* much internal jargon without a translation. I kind of want the register to be very much *like* the Fundamental Intuitions (which we just call that, but we have [EXTENDED date] [ORIGINAL date])... and feature right up top/front. But we're talking to people who might not even know they've clicked on a physics site. *And* we have a DAMN good story. So we need the punchy and the splainy almost side-by-side, but visually distinguishable enough for the scientists to skip the pitch and head for the meat. [And I emphasize here again--take *me* literally; but do NOT literalize instructions into content... I don't need "The Meat Ledger" lol]... speaking of: "Ledger"... eh, LLMese. Humans spot that from a mile away. So... *human* is the aim... scientific human, careful, meticulous (lol) human (I can *act* meticulous... and a human that knows how to show his personality in *any* register/context, and knows how to walk the line and glefully breach it where he pleases because it just works better right here to do that. Overall... my voice should read as my voice. Just my presentor voice who speaks to scientists and children in the same crowd but switches mode in the moment and for the occasion... a guy who knows when mentioning string theory should get a wink and when it shouldn't and how to not make string theory the butt of the joke but to really get... yes, string theory is too big, they mapped out the *whole* space. That's important. And there's probably a lot to learn in all of that. But, it's also part of the job of SAT/H(s)H, *probably*, with humility, to say... *we* have a place for some of string theory, as far as we know. Maybe a lot more, but right now we see *this* intersection as *the* main place for string theory... but pants are part of worldtubes to and we haven't quite gotten to that just yet. And who knows what else. Same for all of physics, and ultimately, necessarily, all of science. We know that's big. We know that's borderline crazy. But we also know what we're doing... is kinda simple: Map first. Name if we have to. Describe/analyze/propose later. << That's the sort of *thinking* that should go into the descriptions/explanations, *and* the design... but those are two different thing, and content drives design. And our content is ...voluptuous? eh... our content is voluminous, diverse, and has many different pitches and modes and sincerity levels and certitudes and styles and purposes, one of which is the overriding one (or two or three maybe, but prioritized, and tailored for the audience--think like each individual audient, and write what a person *wishes* somebody explained that way from the start... which means different things for different audients). 

The "See it/Read it/etc" is good, and maybe we can get a few more tiles in here so this ir really a launchpad for a lot of the site? 
I like the red numbers to indicate "read in this order" under the "how to read" scroller... but it's not entirely clear that that's what they idnicate. Maybe a red "Suggested Read Order" or something to bring it together or maybe just "1st", "2nd"... also the red numbers collide with some of the titles. 
Also... the "visual argument"... uh... isn't. It's a design statement. In general.... let's avoid just clicking anything (esp on the front page), and going to jsut a bigger version of that image. Visual should go to a gallery. The gallery should be a case/argument/education. With simple lables.
ALso, the "two ways in" doesn't do the job exactly. I mean.. Ideally one day we have two full versions of the website... one in physicsese, one in normal peoplese. But for now, maybe a technical library and a browsing library. Which also needs to sort out, or sort to bottom architecture, repo nav/scripts, etc. And we should float to top reccomendeds/importants. 
The provenance theme is also really... not quite what we want on the front page. Maybe as a note for scientists like "Browse technical library and source provenance" > "Techinal library"=presentable, with clickthrogh to raw/provenance. We can jsut simply have a standard datestamp on *all* primary documents *and* their derivatives. That's provenance, no need to point it out. We're kind of doing something like that, but we need to be more systematic and slick. And generally *all* of the reading library fodder should go through a presentability sort and filter/"pay extra attention to getting the *look* clean, and sort of "source-clear" to contextualize the register/content (eg papers/statements/such should look like papers/memos/press releases, conversations should look like conversations.... but in the conversation browser, they're really like looking over the shoulder of a conversation, and in the browsing library they look kind of more like a printed out conversation... or something like that. Ultimately, library/conversation viewer are just two skins on the same material. The former should emphasize (or even limit to) call-outs and important moments. [Which, btw... there *is* a schema for flagging in the original convo viewer documentation... which I *think* is almost designed as a "drop this in *while* you're having the chat" rather than "mark high points and notable things". Ultimately, it would be nice if we could implement our original plan (which was supposed to have been implemented but doesn't seem to have) of a back-end or just "only appears to nathan / nathan's account" tagging system right in the conversations, like (milestone/interesting/funny/demote/promote/hide, etc). ALso on the viewer... Nathan's text scrolls and types at ideal speed. Works less well for assistant. Too fast. Assistant should be fast*er* but not so fast you can't read it. Maybe 2x? Nathan speed? A little detail that was also supposed to have been implemented: A *tiny* (code-minimal) randomization that adds variable typiing speed... though *cadence* is probably a beter term, ideally... with maybe an occasional delete randomly no farther than begining of word feature to make it more human. With the assistant, it's still too fast... which is a problem with the material... big chunks... it still types then jumps then types then jumps for some reason. Lastly on the convo viewer--maybe lastly for now altogether--I'd like the *main* conversation search bar to search not just conversation title, but also within conversations (with Nathan/LLM/other option and date range maybe or earliest/all or something like that). The conversation titles often don't say much about the content. So maybe search is just fully individual message based (or with title search optional or pulls everything, marked as conversation or content)... then clicking takes you to that point in the conversation and the conversation title is up top... something along those lines. Ideally full boolean, with good math handling (and generally we want robust math handling in terms of search *and* presentation... multiple formats and common corruptions (eg:
a
+
b
=
c .... and \_$ sort of stuff, whether LaTeX or markdown or other [perhaps even plaintext] > nice math display with all the bells and whistles, and abiliy to handle odd choices) ...it all gets fixed for presentation *format* wise. ...or at least the LLM's does. I rarely type equations, except copypasta, but that's where the format bugs out)

LLM REVIEWER:

Yes. I think “stale” is the right *felt symptom*, but after going through the site I’d diagnose it more precisely as **runtime staleness / live-system ambiguity**, not stale content.

The actual editorial content is extremely current: the homepage says it was updated September 23, the update log has September 23 entries, the active-work language reflects the present paper push, and the roadmap is reconciled to September 22. ([The Glass Sausage Factory][1]) What makes it feel stale is that a site presenting itself as a living research instrument repeatedly exposes machinery that appears not to be alive.

And yes, your audio suspicion is basically right. The GitHub Pages Conversation Viewer has replay controls, but its documented modes are Cruise, Message replay, and simulated Typealong replay—not listen-along/audio. ([satobloc.github.io][2])  Meanwhile the Glass site says the featured conversation has “per-turn audio,” and the September 22 update says JSON conversations gained role voices and that readable pages gained browser-native audio controls. ([The Glass Sausage Factory][1]) So the public presentation is presently promising a more unified audio experience than the actual HsH viewer supplies.

I went through the main surface plus the dedicated Reading Room, Papers, manuscript display, Updates, Podcast Index, Living Glossary, Claims Explorer, Roadmap, Origin Story, and the HsH Conversation Viewer. I could inspect the live document structures, controls, content, routes, and repository-side viewer implementation. I did **not** get a trustworthy pixel-rendering browser for every page in this environment, so I’m not going to invent opinions about a five-pixel margin or a particular hover effect I couldn't actually see. The structural/presentation issues are much larger than that anyway.

My priority order would be:

1. **Fix the distinction between “live,” “loading,” “unavailable,” and “not built yet.”** This is the biggest thing. The homepage currently exposes “Loading work feed…,” “Loading current work…,” “Loading news feed…,” “Loading headlines…,” “Loading worker submissions…,” etc. ([The Glass Sausage Factory][1]) The Updates page likewise says these things are loaded from the public repository “on each visit” and then exposes three separate `Loading…` states. ([The Glass Sausage Factory][3]) Papers says “Checking current paper status…”. The manuscript says “Loading manuscript… / Verifying source text… / Loading contents…”. The Reading Room says “Loading reader…”. ([The Glass Sausage Factory][4]) Any one of these is normal. Collectively, they make the whole site feel like a demo whose JavaScript stopped halfway through booting.

   I would impose one sitewide state machine: **LIVE · snapshot timestamp**, **CACHED · last successful refresh**, **EXPERIMENTAL**, **OFFLINE**, or **NOT YET CONNECTED**. If a fetch fails, display the most recent cached payload with “snapshot from 18:42 EDT,” not an eternal loading message. The roadmap already demonstrates exactly the intellectual discipline I want here: it explicitly says public direct Mersearch querying waits on a stable API rather than pretending the endpoint exists. ([The Glass Sausage Factory][5]) Make the entire UI behave that way.

2. **Stop making the homepage carry the entire civilization at once.** I actually like a great deal of the homepage. “Start anywhere,” the visual/read/hear/trace division, the curious-reader/scientist-reader fork, epistemic labeling, direct source routes, and the mixture of current activity with historical record are all very appropriate to this project. ([The Glass Sausage Factory][1]) I would absolutely *not* sanitize this into a tasteful five-section academic portfolio.

   But the page is currently roughly 550 crawl lines and successively becomes: front door → research dashboard → featured conversation → audience router → memoir → FIE primer → podcast catalogue → operations board → science-news comparator → methodological statement → repository guide → history → translation desk → reading-room advert → image archive → papers → conversation archive → roadmap. It is almost a complete website vertically serialized into one document. The result isn't information overload so much as **hierarchy decay**. Once I am halfway down, everything has approximately the same rhetorical weight.

   I’d make the homepage a genuinely dynamic newspaper/front desk. Give the first screen and a half the best material **today**. Then provide strong portals into the deep systems instead of partially reproducing each system below.

3. **Let the “currentness” of the site be visible at a glance.** You already have the raw ingredients. I’d make the top portion feel almost like a strange scientific newspaper:

   `THE GLASS SAUSAGE FACTORY`
   current active edge / one-line state
   **one dominant current story or object**
   a compact scrolling strip of genuinely current headlines
   2–4 smaller current cards
   then the four big entrances: SEE / READ / HEAR / TRACE.

   The current “Updated 23 September 2026” is useful, but it is document metadata. ([The Glass Sausage Factory][1]) What I want is perceptual evidence that the *organism is breathing*: “3 worker packets since yesterday,” “paper R1 posted,” “active edge: …,” “latest conversation: …,” “321 podcast episodes,” “feed refreshed 7:14 PM.” Not all of those literally; enough to make life obvious.

4. **Treat the Conversation Viewer as an instrument deserving its own serious UX pass.** Its underlying archival design is actually quite good. It preserves raw source, follows conversation branches, progressively renders long conversations, supports search, deep links, timeline position, speaker colors, previous/next navigation, cross-repository discovery and provenance annotation.  That is not a toy.

   But the public first impression is currently a very utilitarian control panel: conversation filter, Development/Live toggles, hamburger, Prev/Next/Copy link, search, hit count, slider, replay controls, Mode, Speed, View, Show internals, status—before one has even begun reading. ([satobloc.github.io][2]) That makes sense for *us*. For somebody following “Conversation Viewer” from the public site, it is closer to opening a diagnostic console.

   I’d split it conceptually into **Reading** and **Instrument** modes. Reading mode: title, date/span, speakers, clean conversation, search, progress, previous/next, source, and—when actually operational—listen. Instrument mode reveals corpus selection, internals, typealong, provenance controls, dense timeline machinery, branches, etc. Nothing is lost; the complexity simply appears when it becomes useful.

5. **Then make listen-along genuinely first-class—or remove it from the promise until it is.** I would not just bolt speech buttons onto every bubble. The right version is a continuous reader: play/pause, previous/next turn, current speaker, speed, voice mapping, “skip internals,” and a persistent little transport that survives scrolling. Each turn can have its own play affordance, but the principal metaphor should be **listen to the conversation**, not 800 unrelated TTS buttons. The current archive's distinction among user/assistant/system/tool/developer makes intelligent skipping especially important. ([satobloc.github.io][2])

   Until that works end-to-end, I would change the Glass copy from “per-turn audio” to something truthful like “audio-enabled reading views are being integrated,” or hide that bit entirely. A missing feature is fine. A visible button or promise that appears broken makes the *whole product* seem older than it is.

6. **Keep the specialized pages. They are much better than making the homepage do their jobs.** The Podcast Index is one of the cleanest conceptual pages: it establishes scope, counts, eras, search/filter controls, provenance rules and what remains open in only 62 crawl lines. ([The Glass Sausage Factory][6]) The Claims Explorer is also particularly strong: each object has status, differentiator, current check state, dependencies and source routes. ([The Glass Sausage Factory][7]) The Living Glossary has an excellent information architecture—current control / active scaffold / historical translation / recovery target, plus “do not collapse into” and conventional comparison. ([The Glass Sausage Factory][8]) Those are models for the rest of the site.

   In other words: **trust your subpages more**. You don't need the homepage to prove that all this richness exists by reproducing huge chunks of it.

7. **Rationalize the metaphor vocabulary without killing it.** “Glass Sausage Factory,” “factory floor,” “research desk,” “Reading Room,” “paper desk,” “Index Desk,” “public notebook,” “active edge,” “signalbox,” “roadmap,” etc. are individually good. Collectively there are enough architectural metaphors that navigation can become a little Borges library. I would keep the names—they're part of the place—but routinely pair them with tiny functional descriptors:

   **Reading Room · documents & archive**
   **Index Desk · find material**
   **Factory Floor · current work**
   **Signalbox · active priorities**
   **Papers · manuscripts & review**.

   That gives newcomers semantic handrails without converting everything to “Resources / Blog / About.”

8. **The Origin Story should remain enormous, but should become more navigable rather than shorter.** It is 2,700+ crawl lines. ([The Glass Sausage Factory][9]) I don't think the answer is “edit Nathan down to 900 words.” It is a long-form piece; let it be one. But an unobtrusive progress rail, section landmarks, pull-quotes/images, “continue from last place,” and perhaps a contents overlay would make its scale pleasurable instead of merely large. It should feel like a feature essay, not a single HTML text extrusion.

9. **Bring the HsH viewer into the visual family without making it identical.** The Glass site should feel like the magazine/public lobby; the viewer should feel like the archive instrument behind a door in that lobby. At present they read as two separate products. Even just a common masthead treatment, typography variables, source/status badge vocabulary, and a clear “← Glass Sausage Factory” route would make the handoff feel intentional. Conversely, preserving some colder “instrument panel” quality in the viewer would be good. Don't skin it into a magazine article.

The strongest overall impression I got is that **the editorial thinking is ahead of the runtime integration**. This is actually a much better problem than having a polished shell with nothing to say. The Claims page, Glossary, Podcast Index, epistemic labeling, source discipline, historical/current distinctions, and the weird-but-coherent voice are already unusually substantial. ([The Glass Sausage Factory][6])

What is hurting it is that the site currently says, in effect, *“watch the machine work”*—and then several gauges read **LOADING…**

That is why it feels stale even though it was substantially updated **today**.

If I were taking the next design pass, I would therefore **not** start by making things prettier. I would first kill every ambiguous loading state, get the current-work data path robust, reconcile the claimed audio/listen feature with the actual Conversation Viewer, and turn the homepage into a tighter live front page that delegates depth to the genuinely good specialist pages. After that, I’d do the richer visual/ergonomic pass—more asymmetrical modular layout, deliberate scrollers, variable story prominence, long-form reading affordances, and stronger continuity between Glass and the archive instrument.

That would, I think, change the perceived state from **“very ambitious site that may have partly stopped working”** to **“alarmingly large living thing whose unfinished parts are intentionally labeled.”**

[2]: https://satobloc.github.io/HsH/?c=79440217eb99&m=1 "HsH Conversation Viewer"

I think the two takes are actually much more compatible than they initially look. They’re diagnosing different layers.

The LLM reviewer is mostly asking, “How do we make the existing machine behave like a coherent, living website?” You’re asking, “What is this website actually for, and what should a human encounter when they arrive?”

I would do the latter first, then use the former as the engineering discipline underneath it.

The central decision I’d make is:

**The Glass Sausage Factory is not a website about SAT/H(s)H. It is the public interface to the SAT/H(s)H project.**

That distinction is important. It means the front page doesn't need to explain everything. It needs to let a person immediately figure out where they want to go.

And I think your “self-triage” idea is the right organizing principle.

Something roughly like:

**THE GLASS SAUSAGE FACTORY**

*A living research project about the structure of reality.*

Then, almost immediately:

**SEE** — Visual arguments, diagrams, galleries  
**READ** — Research, papers, explanations  
**HEAR** — Conversations, podcasts, audio  
**TRACE** — Sources, history, provenance

And then perhaps:

**EXPLORE SAT** — Basics | Full Overview | Topics | Data  
**EXPLORE H(s)H** — Basics | Full Overview | Topics | Data  
**LIBRARY** — Scientists | Specialists | Everyone  
**NEWS** — The Theory | Related Stories | Archive  
**DRAFTS** — Papers | Theory Work | Press Releases

That is much closer to what I think you're reaching for than either the current front page or the reviewer's proposed “scientific newspaper.”

The newspaper metaphor is useful for one layer of the site—**current activity**—but I wouldn't make it the primary metaphor. A newspaper answers “what's happening today?” Your site has to answer a stranger and more interesting question:

**“What the hell is this, and what can I do with it?”**

And it needs to answer that in about five seconds.

Then the site can become enormous.

### I think we should explicitly separate three things

**1. WAYFINDING**

This is the part that should be almost brutally terse.

SEE  
READ  
HEAR  
TRACE

LIBRARY  
NEWS  
DRAFTS

SAT  
H(s)H

Maybe **START HERE**, but even that might be unnecessary if the architecture itself works.

No paragraphs explaining what the navigation means. The navigation should explain itself.

**2. PITCH**

This is where the unusual story gets told.

Not a giant manifesto. Not “Welcome to the Glass Sausage Factory.” Something that makes a normal intelligent person stop and think:

> Here's the problem. Here's the strange thing we noticed. Here's what we're trying.

And crucially, **the scientist should be able to skip this without feeling punished.**

So you might have a visual relationship like:

**A DIFFERENT WAY TO LOOK AT PHYSICS**

One very short paragraph.

[SEE THE IDEA] [READ THE TECHNICAL VERSION]

That's the “punchy and splainy side-by-side” thing you're describing.

**3. MATERIAL**

This is where the machine gets serious.

Papers should look like papers.

Press releases should look like press releases.

Conversations should look like conversations.

A research document should feel like a research document.

A gallery should feel like a gallery.

A podcast should feel like a podcast.

A conversation transcript should feel like you're looking over somebody's shoulder.

That last point is particularly important. I don't think we should design “the website” as one uniform visual system. We should design a **family resemblance** and then allow each medium to have its own grammar.

That's what “content drives design” really means here.

### And I agree with you strongly about the “RAW” thing

I wouldn't make provenance a theme of the homepage.

It's a property of the material.

A scientist shouldn't have to be told five times that something is transparent. They should encounter a clean document with:

**DATE · VERSION · SOURCE**

and, when appropriate:

**RAW**

That's enough.

Then RAW opens the ugly thing.

That's actually much more powerful than saying:

> We are committed to radical transparency and provenance...

No. Here's the document. Here's the original. Here's what we changed.

Done.

The **Research Library** idea is good for exactly this reason. I especially like the possibility of giving it its own identity:

**GLASS SAUSAGE FACTORY RESEARCH LIBRARY**

*Primary documents, preserved as they are.*

That's almost enough. It has personality without making the library itself into a performance.

And then perhaps:

**CURATED** | **PRIMARY**

rather than “Curated? | Warts and all?”

The latter is a good internal conceptual distinction; the former is probably what the human needs to click.

### The Conversation Viewer is a particularly interesting case

Here I think the reviewer is right almost completely.

But I'd go one step further.

We shouldn't really have one “Conversation Viewer.”

We have **two representations of the same corpus**.

**CONVERSATIONS**

A human-readable archive.

**VIEWER**

The instrument.

That's exactly analogous to your library distinction.

The human version might show:

**WHAT WE WERE THINKING ABOUT**

September 23, 2026  
Nathan + ChatGPT

[conversation]

Not a million controls.

Then:

**SEARCH THIS CONVERSATION**  
**JUMP TO...**  
**LISTEN**

And perhaps a little unobtrusive:

**VIEW SOURCE**

which takes you into the instrument.

Meanwhile the actual HsH Viewer can remain gloriously nerdy.

Search corpus. Branches. Message types. Timeline. Internals. Replay. Provenance. Development/Live. Whatever else.

That is not cruft. That's a different audience.

And I think your “two versions of the website” intuition is actually the deep architecture we should preserve even if we don't literally build two websites:

**PEOPLESE ↔ PHYSICSese**

Everything has to be able to cross that boundary.

A scientist lands on a beautiful explanation and gets:

**TECHNICAL VERSION →**

A curious person lands on a technical document and gets:

**EXPLAIN THIS →**

Neither version is the “dumbed-down” one.

They're different entrances into the same material.

### The reviewer is absolutely right about the loading problem

This is the one place where I would let the reviewer overrule the aesthetic discussion entirely.

“Loading...” is not a design element.

It is an unresolved state.

And because this site is specifically about an ongoing research process, ambiguous runtime state is especially damaging. It makes the project look less alive precisely where we're trying to communicate that it is alive.

So I would establish a hard rule:

**Nothing on the public site gets to say “Loading...” indefinitely.**

Every dynamic object has to resolve to one of:

**LIVE**

**UPDATED [time/date]**

**CACHED [time/date]**

**NOT AVAILABLE**

**IN DEVELOPMENT**

**NOT YET CONNECTED**

That last category is actually fine. In fact, it can become part of the site's personality.

The site doesn't have to pretend everything works.

It has to make it obvious what works.

That gets us to something I think is even more important than “make it look polished”:

**Make incompleteness legible.**

That's very SAT/H(s)H.

### And I would *not* make the homepage much shorter just for the sake of being shorter

The reviewer calls the current homepage “hierarchy decay.”

I think that's exactly right—but I don't think the answer is necessarily deleting the material.

It's **changing the hierarchy.**

There can absolutely be a tremendous amount of stuff below the fold.

The first 20% says:

**Here's what this place is.  
Here's what's happening.  
Here are the doors.**

Then the next 80% can be:

**Oh, you want to wander? Here.**

That distinction is important because one of the site's actual virtues is its abundance.

The Glass Sausage Factory shouldn't look like a tasteful startup landing page.

It should feel a little like you found an unusually well-organized laboratory whose doors all happen to be open.

### And this is where “Nathan as brand” becomes useful

Not Nathan-as-celebrity.

Nathan-as-*authorial intelligence*.

The site should feel like one person made these choices.

Which means the voice can change register without becoming inconsistent.

A physicist gets:

> The construction treats the worldline as the primitive object...

A curious ten-year-old gets:

> Imagine that instead of putting particles *in* spacetime, we started by asking what the particle's history looks like...

And then occasionally:

> Yes, string theory has already explored an absurdly large space of possibilities. That's useful. We're not pretending nobody went there. We're asking whether the geometry we're actually using here gives us a particularly interesting intersection with that space.

And somewhere else:

> Pants are worldtubes too. We haven't worked out the pants yet.

That's not inconsistency.

That's **controlled register switching**.

And I think that's one of the things the site can do that generic scientific websites almost never do: allow a serious scientific project to have an identifiable human mind behind it without turning the science into personality content.

### So, concretely, I think we build this in this order

First, establish the **information architecture** independent of the current page design.

Not CSS. Not animations. Not prettier cards.

Just:

**What are the doors?**

Then establish the **audience pathways**:

curious person →  
interested reader →  
serious reader →  
scientist →  
primary-source researcher

and make sure each can enter and descend naturally.

Then establish the **content grammar**:

paper  
conversation  
podcast  
image  
news item  
claim  
definition  
experiment/data  
press release  
research note

Each gets its own appropriate presentation.

Then establish the **state grammar**:

live / cached / development / unavailable / source.

Then make the backend genuinely editable.

And *then* let Sites do what it's actually good at: helping us shape the presentation rather than being the place where the site's underlying reality lives.

That last part of your first paragraph is important. If you're going to have a weekly allotment of Sites “work,” we shouldn't spend it asking Sites to manually maintain a research database.

The architecture should ideally be:

**repository / structured content → backend data → presentation layer**

with you able to modify the underlying content yourself.

Then the website becomes a renderer.

That gives you something much more valuable than a pretty site: **a website you can actually operate.**

And ultimately I think the governing principle should be very simple:

**The front page is not the website. It is the map.**

The website is everything behind the map.

And the map should be extraordinarily good.
